newsitem.title: UK: Data torrent may even down computer aces - expert.
newsitem.headline: Data torrent may even down computer aces - expert.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent

Information technology embracers are likely to be top dogs next century, but even those manoeuvring into power on the back of the Internet could be overwhelmed by avalanches of data, an American expert said Thursday.
Marian Salzman of New York based advertising agency TBWA International said children who are not educated in the use of computers and the Internet could form a new underclass.
And computerphobes stumbling to master their new machines can take heart. It might not be your fault.
Manufacturers have been guilty of bringing unreliable and overhyped new models to market, she said in an interview.

Salzman, with the enviable title of Worldwide Director, Department of the Future, at TBWA, has advised President Clinton on children's issues, and worked for Japanese computer games powerhouse Nintendo and photo giant Kodak.

The ease with which people will be able to communicate using the Internet, the worldwide network of computers linked by telephone lines, poses dangers. The simplicity and ubiquity of systems means standards of information accuracy may drop.

"Newsgroups on the Internet are really gossip. In the old days, you'd gossip over the fence and it would take two and half months to get to the next village. Now the instant power of gossip is changing our sense of the news," Salzman said.

Last November former White House spokesman Pierre Salinger stirred up controversy by repeating a second-hand theory that had long been available on the Internet. This claimed a U.S. government document proved that a U.S. missile accidentally shot down TWA Flight 800, which crashed off Long Island killing all 230 people on board.
Crash investigators dismissed this information as "unadulterated nonsense".
Salzman worries that computers will become indispensible, and will condemn the "have-nots" to second rate lives.

"You will have technology "haves" and "have-nots", and then you will see stratification within both groups. I think the real worry on a global basis is that the technologies are going to further level-up people."
"If you are a middle class child you have access to the world's libraries at your fingertips, the Smithsonian museum or the British museum, or the Louvre."
This is likely to be less of a problem in the U.S. than in Europe because at least one-third of American familes have computers, with a high proportion connected to the Internet.
Less than 20 percent of European homes have PCs, with only three to four pct on-line.
Some worry that using computers might make work easier, but there was serious downside.
"The more you embrace technology on a practical user level, the more afraid of its implications you become."

"There is a lack of privacy, a feeling that you are never really away from your job. You are information overloaded on one level but that you couldn't possibly have enough time or enough skill to actually find the information you need," Salzman said.
Computer makers, particularly Japanese and U.S., have let the public down.

"We're resigned to the fact that when we buy something new its not going to be perfect. You have to buy the third generation. The first generation is the hype product, the second generation corrects most public flaws, and the third generation works, but then there's the new Wow! product in the shops."
